paragraphs.heading: Open water inside the ice
paragraphs.text: A polynya is an area of open water with sea ice all around it. As a geographical term it means a patch of unfrozen seawater inside pack ice or fast ice that would otherwise be continuous. The word is borrowed from Russian, where it refers to a natural ice hole. Polar explorers adopted it in the 19th century to describe parts of the sea they could navigate.

paragraphs.heading: Two main types
paragraphs.text: There are two main types. Coastal polynyas can be found all year near the Antarctic and Arctic coasts, and are mainly made by strong winds that push the ice away from the shore. Mid-sea polynyas, also called open-ocean polynyas, turn up more sporadically in the middle of the ice pack in certain places, especially around Antarctica. Among the most famous of these is the Weddell Polynya, which opens over the Maud Rise seamount in the Lazarev Sea. It was first spotted in September 1973, lasted through the winters of 1974 to 1976, and recurred in September 2017.

paragraphs.heading: How wind and warmth open them
paragraphs.text: A latent heat polynya is made by katabatic winds, which push ice away from a fixed edge, for example a coastline. First-year pack ice is pushed away from the coast, leaving open water where new ice forms. That new ice is herded downwind in turn until it reaches the pack ice and is consolidated onto it, and the process keeps going. A sensible heat polynya is different: it typically occurs when warm water rising from below keeps the surface water at or above the freezing point, which reduces ice production and may stop it altogether. Mid-sea polynyas form when particular atmospheric conditions occur over preconditioned ocean areas, and polar cyclones are a typical trigger, since their winds drive the ice apart, in opposite directions away from the center of the cyclone.

paragraphs.heading: Ice factories and sinking brine
paragraphs.text: In the Antarctic, latent heat polynyas are one of the major places where sea ice is produced. Their high rate of ice production puts a large amount of brine into the surface water, and this salty water then sinks. Coastal polynyas are in this way a source of Antarctic bottom water, the dense, high-salinity water of the Southern Ocean that plays a major role in the global overturning circulation. For the Arctic, it is an open question whether polynyas can make enough dense water to form a major part of what is needed to drive the thermohaline circulation.

paragraphs.heading: Blooms in the gap
paragraphs.text: Open water in an otherwise ice-covered area can lead to a local bloom of marine algae, called a polynya bloom. The main drivers are sunlight and nutrients. Without sea ice on top, light reaches deeper into the water, and a polynya typically forms together with upwelling, which carries nutrient-rich water from the ocean bottom toward the surface. Phytoplankton grow faster there than in the surrounding ice-covered waters. Primary producers are the base of the marine food web, so polynyas become a critical source of food for fish, birds and marine mammals.

paragraphs.heading: Animals and people who rely on them
paragraphs.text: Some polynyas open at the same time and place every year, and animals can adapt their life strategies to that regularity. The North Water Polynya, between Greenland and Canada, is one of these. Of the Adélie penguin colonies in eastern Antarctica, 91% are linked to a coastal polynya, and polynya size often correlates with colony size. In years when the Ross Sea Polynya did not open, increased seal mortality rates were observed. Polynyas have supported people too: the North Water Polynya, the Arctic's largest and most biologically productive, has been a critical food source in a region that is otherwise barren, enabling high-latitude human communities to exist there for thousands of years.
